laws.title: Absolute Zero Tolerance for Drink Driving
laws.subtitle: Russian Traffic Code — 0.0g/L since 2010
laws.fullDescription: Russia re-introduced absolute zero tolerance for drink driving in 2010 (after a brief relaxation). Any detectable alcohol is illegal. Major crackdown campaigns regularly conducted.
laws.penalty: Any detectable alcohol: fine ₽30,000 + 18-month licence suspension. Repeat: criminal prosecution + fine ₽200,000–₽300,000.
exceptions: None

quiz.q: Russia's BAC limit for drivers?
quiz.explanation: Russia has absolute zero tolerance — any detectable alcohol is illegal since 2010.

laws.title: LGBTQ+ Laws — Propaganda Law Expanded 2023
laws.subtitle: 'Gay propaganda' law expanded to all ages in 2023
laws.fullDescription: Russia's 2013 'gay propaganda' law (banning 'promotion' of non-traditional sexual relations to minors) was dramatically expanded in 2023 to ban such 'propaganda' for all ages. 'The LGBT Movement' was declared extremist in Russia in 2023. Public same-sex affection can lead to arrest. This significantly affects both Russian citizens and foreign visitors.
laws.penalty: 'Gay propaganda': fines up to ₽400,000 for individuals; foreigners can be detained and deported. Extremism charges: up to 6 years.
exceptions: None in practice — discretionary enforcement

quiz.q: What major expansion of Russia's LGBTQ+ restrictions occurred in 2023?
options: The 'propaganda' ban was extended from minors to all ages
quiz.explanation: In 2023, Russia expanded its 'gay propaganda' law from minors to cover all ages, and declared 'the LGBT movement' an extremist organisation.

laws.title: Anti-War Speech Laws 2022 — Discrediting the Army
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code Art. 280.3 — Up to 15 years for spreading 'false' information
laws.fullDescription: Since March 2022, Russia has enacted emergency laws making it a criminal offence to 'discredit' the Russian armed forces or spread 'false information' about military operations (the Ukraine invasion is officially called a 'special military operation' — calling it a war is illegal). Journalists, protesters, and social media users have been arrested. Foreign nationals are not exempt.
laws.penalty: Discrediting the army: up to 7 years. Spreading 'false information' about military: up to 15 years if causing 'grave consequences'.
exceptions: None in practice for public statements

quiz.q: What is officially illegal to call Russia's military action in Ukraine?
options: A war — the official term is 'special military operation'
quiz.explanation: Russia's 2022 law makes it illegal to call the Ukraine invasion a 'war' — the mandatory term is 'special military operation.' Violations carry up to 15 years.

laws.title: Photography — Military, Official Buildings and Border Areas Banned
laws.subtitle: Federal Law No. 5485-1 — State secrets; photographing officials risky
laws.fullDescription: Russia prohibits photography of military installations, government buildings designated as 'strategic objects', border crossings, transport infrastructure (metro interiors in Moscow and St Petersburg are technically restricted), and nuclear facilities. Photographing police or officials without consent can lead to detention. Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) has broad powers to detain and question anyone suspected of intelligence gathering. Foreign visitors have been detained for apparently innocuous photography. Using drones near cities or government buildings is heavily restricted and requires advance permits.
laws.penalty: Photography of state secrets: up to 20 years imprisonment for espionage charges. Photographing police: possible detention. Drone without permit: confiscation + fine.
exceptions: Tourist sites, famous landmarks like Red Square are generally permitted
Professional media with accreditation

quiz.q: Why should tourists be particularly careful about photography in Moscow's metro?
options: The lighting is too dark for photos
The metro system is technically a classified state object — photography is restricted
Photography is only allowed in designated carriages
quiz.explanation: Moscow and St Petersburg's metro systems are technically classified as strategic state objects — photography inside is officially restricted, though enforcement is inconsistent for tourists.

laws.title: Cannabis — Absolutely Illegal; Harsh Penalties
laws.subtitle: Russian Criminal Code — Any amount: criminal offence
laws.fullDescription: Cannabis is absolutely illegal in Russia with no decriminalisation. Possession of any amount can lead to criminal charges. Russia has extremely harsh drug laws — foreigners (including tourists) have been imprisoned for long sentences for drug offences. Even small quantities found in luggage can lead to arrest. In 2023, American basketball player Brittney Griner was released after being jailed for 9 months for cannabis vape cartridges — a high-profile case showing enforcement applies to foreigners. Russia uses the concept of 'significant amount' which is defined very broadly.
laws.penalty: Possession of any cannabis: administrative fine + criminal charges possible. 'Significant amount' (6+ grams): 3–10 years imprisonment. Trafficking: up to 20 years.
exceptions: No exceptions — no medical cannabis, no decriminalisation
laws.sourceLabel: Russian Criminal Code Art. 228 — Drug Offences

quiz.q: What happened to US basketball player Brittney Griner in Russia?
options: She was imprisoned for 9 months for cannabis vape cartridges before being released in a prisoner swap
She was given a warning only
quiz.explanation: Brittney Griner was arrested at Moscow airport in 2022 and imprisoned for 9 months for cannabis vape cartridges — before being released in a high-profile prisoner exchange with Viktor Bout.

laws.title: Russia's LGBTQ+ Laws — 'Gay Propaganda' Ban Expanded to All Ages (2023)
laws.subtitle: Federal Law No. 135-FZ (amended 2023) — LGBTQ 'movement' declared extremist
laws.fullDescription: Russia's original 'gay propaganda' law, passed in 2013, banned the 'promotion of non-traditional sexual relationships' to minors — a law condemned internationally but which had an immediate chilling effect on LGBTQ+ visibility and rights. In December 2022, Russia's Supreme Court dramatically expanded the restriction to apply to all audiences regardless of age, effectively banning any positive depiction or discussion of LGBTQ+ relationships in public. Then in November 2023, the Russian Supreme Court went further, declaring the entire 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation — a designation that in theory could criminalise private expressions of LGBTQ+ identity. Rainbow flags, same-sex affection in public, and even rainbow-coloured clothing have led to detentions. These laws apply equally to foreign visitors, and several tourists have been detained. Same-sex partnerships have never been legally recognised in Russia and a 2020 constitutional amendment banned same-sex marriage.
laws.penalty: Individual displaying LGBTQ+ 'propaganda': administrative fine of up to ₽400,000. Foreigners: administrative fine + detention + deportation. Under the extremism declaration, potential criminal charges for participation in LGBTQ+ activities.
exceptions: No formal exceptions exist — enforcement is inconsistent but has become more aggressive since 2022
Private expressions in strictly private settings are less frequently targeted, though the law technically covers these
laws.sourceLabel: Federal Law No. 135-FZ — Russian 'Gay Propaganda' Law and 2023 Amendments

quiz.q: In what year did Russia expand its 'gay propaganda' law from applying only to minors to applying to all ages?
quiz.explanation: Russia's original 2013 'gay propaganda' law applied only to minors. In December 2022, the Russian parliament voted to expand it to cover all ages — making any positive depiction of LGBTQ+ relationships illegal in any public context. The Supreme Court then declared the 'LGBT movement' extremist in 2023.

laws.title: VPN and Foreign Agent Laws — Internet Restricted; Criticism Criminalised
laws.subtitle: Roskomnadzor — 300,000+ sites blocked; 'war' is a criminal word
laws.fullDescription: Russia's internet ('Runet') is increasingly isolated from the global web. Roskomnadzor has blocked over 300,000 websites, including Instagram, Facebook, BBC, and many VPN services. The 'Foreign Agent' law (expanded 2020–2022) requires individuals receiving foreign funding who engage in 'political activity' to label all their content as produced by a foreign agent. Under 2022 wartime laws, sharing 'false information' about the Russian military (e.g. calling the invasion of Ukraine a 'war' rather than 'special military operation') carries up to 15 years imprisonment. Russia's sovereign internet law (2019) allows the Kremlin to disconnect Runet from the global internet entirely.
laws.penalty: Calling the Ukraine war a 'war': up to 15 years. Discrediting the Russian army: up to 5 years. Foreign agent violation: fines to criminal charges.
exceptions: Government-sanctioned media and official state communications
Diplomatic missions operate under separate legal frameworks
laws.sourceLabel: Freedom House — Freedom on the Net: Russia 2023

quiz.q: What does Russia officially call its military operation in Ukraine, with criminal penalties for using any other term?
quiz.explanation: Russia officially calls its invasion of Ukraine the 'Special Military Operation' — using the words 'war' or 'invasion' in public or on social media can result in criminal prosecution under 2022 laws.

laws.title: Russian Customs Rules — Antiques, Currency and Banned Imports
laws.subtitle: Federal Customs Service — Antiques pre-1945: export licence required
laws.fullDescription: Russia's customs rules are strict and apply to both entry and exit. Exporting antiques, artworks, or cultural objects manufactured before 1945 requires a cultural values export licence from the Ministry of Culture — without it, the item will be confiscated at the border and the exporter prosecuted. Caviar can be exported in amounts up to 250g per person (for personal use). Cash above USD $10,000 must be declared. Certain medications common in Western countries (including some sleeping pills, ADHD medications, and codeine-based painkillers) are classified as narcotics in Russia and cannot be brought in without advance declaration and documentation. Religious literature that could be considered 'extremist' under Russian law may be confiscated.
laws.penalty: Undeclared antique export: criminal charges + confiscation. Undeclared cash over $10,000: up to 50% confiscation. Bringing undeclared narcotics: up to 10 years.
exceptions: Accredited diplomatic pouches for embassy personnel
Licensed antique dealers with Ministry of Culture export permit
laws.sourceLabel: Federal Customs Service of Russia — Customs Rules

quiz.q: How much caviar can a traveller legally export from Russia for personal use?
quiz.explanation: Russian customs allows up to 250 grams of caviar per person for personal export — exceeding this amount requires documentation of commercial or gift purpose and may be subject to additional duties or restrictions.

laws.title: 'Foreign Agent' Law — NGOs, Media, and Individuals Face Harsh Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Russia's expanding foreign agent laws impose stigmatizing labels and crushing compliance burdens
laws.fullDescription: Russia's Foreign Agent Law (2012, extensively amended 2017, 2019, 2020, 2022) originally targeted NGOs receiving foreign funding. Subsequent expansions covered: media organizations, unregistered civil society groups, individual journalists and bloggers, and ultimately anyone 'under foreign influence' — even without receiving foreign money. 'Foreign agents' must label all communications with lengthy disclaimers, submit quarterly financial reports, and undergo annual audits. The label carries Soviet-era connotations of espionage and treason. Memorial International — Russia's oldest human rights organization — was dissolved in 2021 under the law. Post-2022 Ukraine invasion: the law was weaponized against anti-war voices; 'discrediting the army' became a separate criminal offense (up to 15 years imprisonment).
laws.penalty: Operating as unregistered foreign agent: fines up to 500,000 rubles + criminal charges (up to 5 years). 'Discrediting the army': up to 15 years. Spreading 'false information' about military: up to 15 years.
exceptions: State-owned media and organizations under government control
Religious organizations with approval from state authorities
Cultural exchange programs specifically approved by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
laws.sourceLabel: Memorial Human Rights Centre — Foreign Agent Law Analysis

quiz.q: What happened to Memorial International — Russia's oldest human rights organization — under the Foreign Agent Law?
options: It was fined but allowed to continue operating
It was forcibly dissolved by court order in 2021
It voluntarily self-dissolved to protect its members
It relocated to Germany and continued operations
quiz.explanation: Memorial International, Russia's oldest and most respected human rights organization (founded 1989), was forcibly dissolved by Russian court order in December 2021 under the Foreign Agent Law — a landmark case that signaled intensifying restrictions on civil society before the 2022 Ukraine invasion.

laws.title: Ukraine War Mobilization Laws — Partial Mobilization, Desertion, and Anti-War Speech
laws.subtitle: Russia mobilized 300,000 reservists in September 2022; new criminal penalties for anti-war speech
laws.fullDescription: Russia's September 21, 2022 partial mobilization decree called up approximately 300,000 reservists for the Ukraine war — triggering the largest emigration wave since the Bolshevik Revolution, with an estimated 700,000+ Russians leaving in the following months. The Criminal Code was amended: discrediting the Russian armed forces (Article 20.3.3): up to 15 years imprisonment; spreading 'false information' about the military (Article 207.3): up to 15 years; calling for actions against state security: up to 20 years. Desertion during wartime: 5–15 years. Voluntary surrender: 3–10 years. Conscripts cannot refuse deployment orders. Over 16,000 people faced charges under new anti-war laws by early 2024. Participating in unauthorized protests against mobilization: up to 15 years.
laws.penalty: Discrediting armed forces: up to 15 years (media cases: harsher). Desertion: 5–15 years. Voluntary surrender: 3–10 years. Anti-war social media posts: criminal prosecution + detention.
exceptions: Diplomatic communications through official channels
Academic analysis in state-approved institutions (self-censorship is near-universal)
Medical exemptions from mobilization with documented conditions
laws.sourceLabel: Human Rights Watch — Russia War Crimes and Mobilization 2023

quiz.q: How many Russians approximately left the country after Russia's September 2022 partial mobilization decree?
quiz.explanation: An estimated 700,000+ Russians left the country in the months following the September 2022 partial mobilization decree — the largest emigration wave since the Bolshevik Revolution. Many crossed to Georgia, Kazakhstan, Finland (before border closure), and other neighboring countries to avoid conscription.

laws.title: War Censorship Laws — Ukraine Invasion
laws.subtitle: Laws criminalizing 'discrediting' the military or calling it a 'war' carry 15-year sentences
laws.fullDescription: Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, the Russian government rapidly passed laws criminalizing public opposition. Article 20.3.3 (discrediting the armed forces) carries up to 15 years imprisonment; calling the 'special military operation' a 'war' can itself constitute a violation. Thousands were arrested at anti-war protests. Independent media was shuttered — Novaya Gazeta suspended, Echo Moskvy liquidated, TV Rain fled to Latvia. Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter were blocked. VPN use surged but authorities moved to restrict VPN providers.
laws.penalty: Discrediting the armed forces: up to 15 years. Spreading 'false information' about the military: up to 15 years. Calling for anti-war protests: criminal charges. Journalists face decade-long sentences.
exceptions: Statements made in private with no public audience have limited exposure
Russian citizens abroad may speak more freely though arrests on return are documented
State-approved media may criticize tactical military decisions within bounds

quiz.q: Under Russian law passed after the Ukraine invasion, what is the maximum sentence for 'discrediting' the Russian armed forces?
quiz.explanation: Russia's post-invasion censorship laws (Article 20.3.3) carry sentences of up to 15 years imprisonment for 'discrediting' the armed forces or spreading 'false information' about military operations.

laws.title: Navalny's Death & Russian Opposition
laws.subtitle: Alexei Navalny died in Arctic penal colony in February 2024 — Putin's most prominent critic silenced
laws.fullDescription: Alexei Navalny, Russia's most prominent opposition leader, died in IK-6 'Polar Wolf' Arctic penal colony on February 16, 2024. He had survived a Novichok nerve agent poisoning in 2020 (survived through German hospital treatment) and voluntarily returned to Russia in 2021, where he was immediately arrested. His death — officially 'natural causes' — was internationally condemned as a Kremlin assassination; his widow Yulia Navalnaya vowed to continue his work. The Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK) he founded, which exposed Kremlin corruption including Putin's alleged $1.4 billion 'Palace on the Sea,' continues operations from abroad. Russia designated FBK as 'extremist.'
laws.penalty: Participation in FBK activities inside Russia: up to 10 years imprisonment. Donating to FBK: criminal prosecution. Sharing Navalny's content: potential criminal charges for 'rehabilitating extremism.'
exceptions: Russians abroad can support FBK with less legal risk though bank transactions are tracked
Navalny's death triggered intensified crackdowns on remaining domestic opposition
His film 'Navalny' won the 2023 Oscar for Best Documentary

quiz.q: What method was used in the 2020 assassination attempt against Alexei Navalny that he survived?
quiz.explanation: Alexei Navalny was poisoned with the Novichok nerve agent in August 2020 — the same class of chemical weapons used in the Salisbury poisoning in the UK. He survived after emergency treatment in Germany, then voluntarily returned to Russia in 2021 where he was immediately arrested.

laws.title: Wagner Group & Africa Mercenary Operations
laws.subtitle: Russia's private military company spread across Africa after Prigozhin's death, rebranded as Africa Corps
laws.fullDescription: The Wagner Group, Russia's private military company founded by Yevgeny Prigozhin, expanded across Africa from 2018: Libya, Sudan, Central African Republic, Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, and Mozambique. Wagner operations traded military support for ruling regimes in exchange for resource extraction concessions (gold, diamonds). After Prigozhin's mutiny (June 2023) and subsequent plane crash death (August 2023), Wagner was absorbed into Russian military structures and rebranded as the 'Africa Corps' under direct Defense Ministry control. Russian military influence in the Sahel expanded dramatically as French forces were expelled from Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger in 2022–2023.
laws.penalty: Wagner mercenaries operating in Africa have no legal accountability in Russia — private military companies were technically illegal in Russia until 2023. Resource extraction under Wagner-protected regimes bypasses international transparency standards.
exceptions: Diplomatic personnel from Russia in African countries have immunity
Arms deliveries to African governments are legal under bilateral agreements
Wagner-affiliated gold from CAR and Sudan can be sold through UAE intermediaries

quiz.q: What happened to the Wagner Group after leader Yevgeny Prigozhin died in a plane crash in August 2023?
options: Wagner was absorbed into Russian military structures and rebranded as the Africa Corps
Wagner became fully independent from Russia
Wagner merged with a Chinese private military company
quiz.explanation: After Prigozhin's death, the Wagner Group was absorbed into Russian Defense Ministry structures and rebranded as the 'Africa Corps' — maintaining and expanding its operations across the Sahel as French forces were expelled and Russian influence grew.

laws.title: Wartime Censorship: 'Discrediting the Army' & 15-Year Prison Terms
laws.subtitle: Russia criminalized calling its Ukraine invasion a 'war' — the word itself can result in years of imprisonment
laws.fullDescription: After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the State Duma passed laws within days criminalizing 'discrediting' the Russian armed forces and spreading 'false information' about military operations. The official term 'special military operation' became legally mandatory — calling the invasion a 'war' could constitute an offense. 'Discrediting the army' carries up to 15 years imprisonment for acts committed 'with grave consequences.' Russians have been arrested for holding blank signs, for private social media posts visible to few followers, and for anti-war art installations. Independent media was shut down; Novaya Gazeta suspended publication. Over 800,000 Russians fled the country in the first year.
laws.penalty: 'Discrediting the army': up to 15 years imprisonment. 'False information' about military operations: up to 15 years. Calling for 'action against state security': up to 20 years
exceptions: State-approved criticism of logistics failures (not the war itself) has been tolerated to some degree
Russian military bloggers ('milbloggers') have more latitude than civilians to criticize military tactics

quiz.q: What specific word did Russia's post-invasion censorship laws effectively criminalize?
quiz.explanation: Russia's laws mandating the use of 'special military operation' effectively criminalized calling the Ukraine invasion a 'war' — a word that could be construed as spreading 'false information' about military operations, carrying up to 15 years imprisonment.

laws.title: Alexei Navalny: Death in Arctic Prison & Russia's Assassination Laws
laws.subtitle: Russia's most prominent opposition leader died in Arctic prison in February 2024 — Western governments said Putin was responsible
laws.fullDescription: Alexei Navalny — Russia's most prominent opposition leader, anti-corruption crusader, and Putin's most visible domestic critic — died in IK-6 'Polar Wolf' Arctic prison on February 16, 2024. He had survived a 2020 Novichok nerve agent poisoning (carried out by FSB agents, per Bellingcat investigation) and was serving a combined 19-year sentence on what Western governments called politically motivated charges. The day he died, he reportedly appeared healthy at a court hearing. Russian authorities attributed his death to 'natural causes.' The US, UK, EU, and dozens of governments attributed responsibility to Putin. His widow Yulia Navalnaya vowed to continue his work.
laws.penalty: Navalny's sentences: 'extremism' (19 years), plus earlier fraud and parole violation convictions. Under Russian law, criticizing his prosecution was itself a criminal risk
exceptions: Russia's Federal Penitentiary Service claimed standard medical protocols were followed
No independent autopsy was permitted; his body was held for weeks before being returned to family

quiz.q: How did Alexei Navalny survive a 2020 assassination attempt before his eventual death in prison in 2024?
options: He survived Novichok nerve agent poisoning — attributed to FSB agents by investigators
He escaped a prison transfer by bribing guards
quiz.explanation: Navalny survived Novichok nerve agent poisoning in August 2020 — an assassination attributed to FSB agents by Bellingcat investigators using flight records and phone data — before dying in Arctic prison in February 2024 under circumstances Western governments attributed to the Putin regime.

laws.title: Law Against Discrediting the Army
laws.subtitle: Russia's 2022 law criminalizes any public criticism of the Ukraine war
laws.fullDescription: Following the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia passed Federal Law No. 32-FZ making it a criminal offense to 'discredit' the Russian army or spread 'false information' about the military. The law was rapidly expanded: calling the invasion a 'war' (rather than the official term 'special military operation'), posting anti-war messages on social media, protesting, or wearing blue and yellow (Ukrainian colors) can result in prosecution. Penalties escalated through subsequent amendments. The law essentially criminalized all public opposition to the war. Russia's media regulator Roskomnadzor blocked major independent media outlets. Over 19,000 people were detained for anti-war protests in the first year.
laws.penalty: Up to 3 years for 'discrediting'; up to 15 years for 'false information' about the military; if causing 'grave consequences' — 15 years
exceptions: No meaningful legal exceptions — the law's vague wording gives prosecutors enormous discretion

quiz.q: What is Russia's official term for its invasion of Ukraine?
quiz.explanation: Russia officially calls its invasion of Ukraine a 'special military operation' (специальная военная операция). Using the word 'war' in public can result in criminal prosecution under Russia's 2022 army discrediting law.

laws.title: Foreign Agent Law
laws.subtitle: Russia's Foreign Agent Law requires organizations to register and label all communications
laws.fullDescription: Russia's Foreign Agents Law (2012, significantly expanded 2017–2022) requires NGOs, media organizations, and individuals who receive foreign funding and engage in 'political activity' to register as 'foreign agents' (inostranny agent) — a term deliberately echoing Soviet-era spy terminology. Registered foreign agents must label all publications, conduct invasive audits, and file detailed reports. The law has been used to designate virtually all independent media and civil society organizations. Most major independent media (Meduza, VTimes, iStories) and human rights groups (Memorial) have been shut down or forced abroad. After the Ukraine invasion, the law was used against ordinary individuals.
laws.penalty: Failure to register as foreign agent: fines of up to RUB 500,000; continuation of activities after designation: criminal prosecution up to 5 years
exceptions: Religious organizations were initially exempt (a status later narrowed)
Government-affiliated organizations are never designated regardless of foreign funding

quiz.q: What Soviet-era term does Russia deliberately use for its 'Foreign Agent' designation?
quiz.explanation: Russia deliberately chose 'inostranny agent' (foreign agent) for its designation — a term deeply associated with Soviet-era espionage and spy prosecutions — to stigmatize civil society organizations and independent media receiving any foreign funding.

laws.title: Foreign Agents Law
laws.subtitle: NGOs and media receiving foreign funding face strict labeling and restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Russia's Foreign Agents Law (originally 2012, significantly expanded 2017–2022) requires any organization or individual receiving foreign funding and deemed to engage in broadly-defined 'political activity' to register as a 'foreign agent,' a Soviet-era term with stigmatizing connotations. Registered entities must label all publications and communications with prominent warnings, submit to extensive audits, and file quarterly financial reports. Since 2022, the law was further expanded to include individuals, media outlets, and foreign-funded entities without requiring proof of foreign direction. Hundreds of civil society organizations, journalists, and independent media have been designated under the law, effectively shuttering many.
laws.penalty: Fines up to 500,000 rubles for individuals; criminal liability (up to 5 years) for repeated violations or failure to register
exceptions: Pure commercial activity may be exempt
Academic and scientific exchanges under specific bilateral agreements

laws.title: Sovereign Internet Law (RuNet)
laws.subtitle: Russia's 2019 law created infrastructure to disconnect the Russian internet from the global web
laws.fullDescription: Russia's Federal Law 'On Communications' amendments (the so-called 'Sovereign Internet Law' or RuNet law), effective November 1, 2019, required Russian internet service providers to install deep packet inspection (DPI) equipment provided by Roskomnadzor (the internet regulator) to enable traffic filtering and routing. The law aimed to allow Russia to operate an autonomous internet ('RuNet') disconnected from the global internet if necessary. The law mandates that all Russian internet traffic passes through Roskomnadzor-controlled exchange points. Combined with the 2022 war in Ukraine (which accelerated Russian internet controls), thousands of websites have been blocked in Russia — including Facebook, Instagram, BBC, Deutsche Welle, and virtually all major Western news sources. Russia has attempted to block services including Tor and VPNs (with mixed success). In 2022, Russia was effectively isolated from many global internet services through commercial decisions by US tech companies and through Russian government blocks.
laws.penalty: ISPs not installing DPI equipment: fines; websites not complying with blocking orders: fines up to 4 million rubles; using prohibited VPNs to access blocked content: fines for services (not yet consistently for users)
exceptions: Government agencies and military have separate secure networks
Academic and research networks have limited exemptions
Critical infrastructure communications have technical carve-outs

laws.title: 2020 Constitutional Amendments and Putin's Term Reset
laws.subtitle: Russia's constitution was amended to allow Putin to rule until 2036
laws.fullDescription: In July 2020, Russia held a nationwide vote on sweeping constitutional amendments proposed by President Vladimir Putin. The amendments, which passed with 78% approval in a vote criticized for procedural violations, reset Putin's presidential term count to zero — allowing him to seek re-election twice more after 2024, potentially remaining in power until 2036. Other changes included banning same-sex marriage, referencing God in the constitution, prioritizing Russian law over international treaties, and expanding social guarantees. Critics called it a constitutional coup. In March 2024, Putin won re-election with 87% of the vote in an election with no credible opposition and heavy repression of dissent.
laws.penalty: Public criticism of the military or 'discrediting' armed forces: up to 15 years imprisonment (amended 2022). Unauthorized protest: up to 15 days detention or large fines.
exceptions: Government-sanctioned political activity permitted
Registered political parties (meeting strict criteria) may field candidates

quiz.q: What did Russia's 2020 constitutional amendments do to Putin's term limits?
options: They imposed a 2-term limit for the first time
They reset his term count to zero, allowing rule until 2036
They reduced presidential terms to 4 years
quiz.explanation: The amendments reset Putin's term count to zero despite his previous terms, allowing him to run for two more 6-year terms after 2024 — potentially ruling until 2036.

laws.title: Navalny's Death and Criminalization of Dissent
laws.subtitle: Russia's most prominent opposition leader died in custody in February 2024
laws.fullDescription: Alexei Navalny, Russia's most prominent opposition leader, died in an Arctic penal colony (IK-6 'Polar Wolf') on February 16, 2024. Russian authorities claimed natural causes; Western governments and Navalny's team blamed the Putin government. Navalny had survived a Novichok nerve agent poisoning in 2020, which he attributed to Russian intelligence. His death followed a series of increasing criminal sentences: first 9 years, then 19 years (extremism), and finally a 2024 conviction that would have kept him imprisoned until 2041. After his death, his organization declared it would continue abroad. Russia had already labeled his Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK) an extremist organization.
laws.penalty: Distributing FBK (Navalny's) materials: up to 10 years imprisonment under extremism laws. Attending unauthorized memorial gatherings for Navalny: up to 15 days administrative detention.
exceptions: No meaningful legal exceptions to political repression in current Russian framework
Diplomatic staff retain immunity — Russian opposition in exile continues work abroad

quiz.q: What was Alexei Navalny best known for in Russia?
options: Leading Russia's Communist Party after the Soviet era
Running an anti-corruption organization exposing government corruption and leading the political opposition
Founding Russia's largest independent news channel
Negotiating peace talks between Russia and Ukraine
quiz.explanation: Navalny led the Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which published viral investigations into Kremlin corruption, and ran for president in 2018 (barred by authorities), making him Russia's most prominent opposition leader.

laws.title: Prigozhin's Mutiny and Wagner Group's Fate
laws.subtitle: Russia's most dramatic internal challenge since 1993 ended mysteriously with Prigozhin's death
laws.fullDescription: On June 23-24, 2023, Yevgeny Prigozhin — leader of the Wagner Group mercenary force that fought in Ukraine and Africa — launched an armed mutiny. Wagner fighters seized Rostov-on-Don and marched toward Moscow before stopping under a deal brokered by Belarusian President Lukashenko. Prigozhin was promised amnesty and exile to Belarus. Two months later, on August 23, 2023, Prigozhin died in a plane crash near Tver — widely attributed to the Putin government. Wagner's operations were absorbed into Russian military structure. The mutiny exposed fractures in Putin's security apparatus and was the most significant internal challenge to his rule in his 23+ year tenure.
laws.penalty: Armed rebellion against the state: up to life imprisonment under Russian Criminal Code. Participation in Wagner after reclassification: potential prosecution under terrorism laws.
exceptions: Fighters who surrendered under amnesty deal technically exempt from prosecution — though enforcement uncertain
Wagner's African operations continued under a rebranded GRU-affiliated structure

quiz.q: How did Yevgeny Prigozhin die, and what was widely believed to be responsible?
options: He was killed in combat operations in Ukraine
He died in a plane crash widely attributed to the Putin government
He was poisoned in exile in Belarus
He was convicted of treason and executed
quiz.explanation: Prigozhin died when his private jet crashed on August 23, 2023 — exactly two months after his mutiny and shortly after returning to Russia. Western governments and most independent analysts widely attributed the crash to the Putin government, though Russia denied involvement.

laws.title: Russian War Censorship and Mobilization Laws
laws.subtitle: Criminalizing dissent from official military narrative
laws.fullDescription: Following Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, sweeping censorship laws were enacted. Federal Law 32-FZ criminalizes 'discrediting' the Russian Armed Forces, punishable by up to 15 years in prison if it leads to 'serious consequences'. Calling the war a 'war' rather than a 'special military operation' is punishable. The September 2022 partial mobilization law requires men 18-65 to report when called up; evading mobilization is criminal. Russian media abroad is labeled 'foreign agents' requiring labeling on all content.
laws.penalty: Discrediting armed forces: up to 15 years. Spreading 'false information' about military: up to 15 years. Mobilization evasion: up to 10 years imprisonment. Calling for anti-war protests: up to 15 years
exceptions: Foreign nationals with valid visas not subject to mobilization
Certain professions (IT, defense industry) may receive deferments
Men with sole custody of dependents may apply for exemption

quiz.q: What is the official Russian government term for the invasion of Ukraine?
quiz.explanation: The Russian government mandates calling it a 'Special Military Operation' — using the word 'war' to describe the conflict in Ukraine is criminalized under Russian censorship laws.

laws.title: Russia's Constitutional Amendments and Term Reset
laws.subtitle: 2020 amendments allowed Putin to potentially rule until 2036
laws.fullDescription: Russia's 2020 constitutional referendum approved sweeping changes including resetting presidential term limits — allowing Vladimir Putin to potentially serve as president until 2036. Other changes: references to Russia as the legal successor of the USSR, prohibition of same-sex marriage, mention of God in the constitution, and primacy of Russian constitutional law over international court rulings. The referendum passed with 77% approval under conditions opposition groups criticized as unfair. In 2024, Putin won re-election with 87% of the vote in an election with no credible opposition candidates.
laws.penalty: Violations of constitutional order: up to life imprisonment. Calling for constitutional change through 'extremist' methods: up to 6 years. Participating in organizations the government calls extremist: up to 10 years. Spreading 'discrediting' information about Putin's elections: up to 5 years
exceptions: Diplomatic personnel retain immunity
Constitutional court justices have formal independence provisions (in practice limited)
Academic constitutional law analysis permitted in controlled institutional settings

quiz.q: Until what year could Vladimir Putin potentially serve as president under Russia's 2020 constitutional amendment?
quiz.explanation: Russia's 2020 constitutional referendum reset Putin's presidential term count to zero, allowing him to run for two more six-year terms and potentially remain president until 2036 — extending what would have been a constitutional term limit.

laws.title: Russia's Foreign Agents and Undesirable Organizations Law
laws.subtitle: Sweeping laws criminalize contact with Western organizations
laws.fullDescription: Russia's foreign agent law (expanded in 2020 and 2022) requires anyone receiving foreign funding or considered to be 'under foreign influence' to register as a foreign agent, label all materials with lengthy warnings, and submit to extensive reporting. The Undesirable Organizations Law (2015) goes further — designating foreign and international organizations as 'undesirable,' making any participation a criminal offense. The US National Endowment for Democracy, Open Society Foundations, and dozens of others have been designated. Russians who participate in activities of undesirable organizations face up to 6 years imprisonment.
laws.penalty: Unregistered foreign agent activity: fines up to 500,000 rubles and imprisonment up to 5 years. Participating in undesirable organization: up to 6 years. Spreading foreign agent materials without warning labels: fines. Failure to report foreign agent activities: up to 2 years
exceptions: Diplomatic staff have immunity
Foreign journalists with accreditation have limited but contested protections
Academic exchange with universities not designated as undesirable may be permitted

quiz.q: What does Russia's Undesirable Organizations Law make illegal?
options: Any participation in activities of designated foreign organizations — criminal offense
quiz.explanation: Russia's Undesirable Organizations Law designates foreign organizations as 'undesirable' and makes any participation in their activities a criminal offense — meaning Russians who participate in programs run by designated organizations like Open Society Foundations can face up to 6 years imprisonment.

laws.title: Foreign Agent Law Expansions and NGO Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Russia dramatically expanded 'foreign agent' designations after 2022
laws.fullDescription: Russia's 'foreign agent' law, originally modeled loosely on the US FARA, has been dramatically expanded since 2022. Any individual, media outlet, or organization receiving foreign funding or deemed to be 'under foreign influence' can be designated a foreign agent. Designated persons must label all their content prominently and submit to intrusive audits. The law was used to shut down Memorial (a leading human rights organization), numerous independent media, and to restrict opposition politicians. After the 2022 Ukraine invasion, the law was further expanded to cover 'undesirable organizations' and to criminalize spreading 'false information' about the Russian military.
laws.penalty: False information about the Russian military: up to 15 years imprisonment; unauthorized foreign agent activity: up to 5 years
exceptions: State-affiliated organizations and Kremlin-approved civil society groups

quiz.q: What can result in a 'foreign agent' designation in Russia after 2022?
options: Only receiving direct foreign government funding
Any foreign funding OR being deemed 'under foreign influence'
quiz.explanation: After 2022 expansions, Russia's foreign agent law can designate anyone receiving foreign funding OR anyone deemed to be 'under foreign influence' — a vague standard that has been applied broadly.

laws.title: Mobilization Laws and Draft Evasion Consequences
laws.subtitle: Russia's partial mobilization law created criminal penalties for draft dodging
laws.fullDescription: Russia's September 2022 partial mobilization decree ordered 300,000 reservists to military service for the Ukraine war. The Criminal Code was amended to dramatically increase penalties for unauthorized departure from service, desertion, and insubordination during wartime. Surrendering to the enemy became a new criminal offense. Draft evasion carries up to 10 years imprisonment. Men of conscription age (18-27) face travel restrictions. Russia also criminalized publicizing information about mobilized soldiers that could 'discredit' the military. The mobilization and related laws forced hundreds of thousands of Russian men to flee to neighboring countries.
laws.penalty: Desertion during mobilization: up to 15 years imprisonment; unauthorized departure from battlefield: up to 10 years; surrender: up to 10 years
exceptions: Medical deferments through official military medical boards
Sole breadwinner exemptions for single fathers

quiz.q: What new military offense did Russia add to its Criminal Code during the Ukraine war?
options: Surrendering to the enemy (became a new criminal offense)
Failing to report for annual reserves checkup
quiz.explanation: Russia added 'surrendering to the enemy' as a new criminal offense to its Criminal Code during the Ukraine war, with penalties up to 10 years imprisonment — part of a package of wartime criminal law amendments.

laws.title: Constitutional Amendments and Putin's Extended Presidency
laws.subtitle: Russia's 2020 constitutional reset allows Putin to rule until 2036
laws.fullDescription: Russia's 2020 constitutional amendments, approved in a national vote, included a 'zeroing out' provision resetting presidential term limits — allowing Vladimir Putin to potentially remain in office until 2036. The amendments also embedded conservative values including the definition of marriage as between a man and woman, referenced God, and prohibited alienation of Russian territory (complicating any peace deal over occupied territories). Subsequent amendments and laws have further embedded wartime legal provisions. The amendments were passed with official claims of 78% support in a vote criticized for procedural violations. Putin was re-elected in 2024 in an election without credible opposition.
laws.penalty: Not directly penal — constitutional changes; but attempting to change the now-constitutionally-enshrined territorial integrity is criminalized
exceptions: Academic analysis of constitutional history permissible within narrow parameters
Diplomatic communications on constitutional interpretation through official channels

quiz.q: Until what year do Russia's 2020 constitutional amendments potentially allow Putin to remain president?
quiz.explanation: Russia's 2020 constitutional amendments 'zeroed out' previous presidential terms with a provision that could allow Putin to remain president until 2036, having served since 2000 with a brief interruption as Prime Minister.

laws.title: Russia War Censorship and Information Control Laws
laws.subtitle: Russia criminalizes unauthorized information about the military
laws.fullDescription: Following the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Russia enacted sweeping laws criminalizing the spread of information that discredits the Russian armed forces, including calling the war a war rather than a special military operation. Penalties reach up to 15 years imprisonment. Thousands have been prosecuted. Independent media outlets were shut down, foreign social media platforms were blocked, and VPN usage surged. The laws have been applied retroactively against historical social media posts.
laws.penalty: Up to 15 years imprisonment for discrediting the military; up to 25 years for treason or espionage; fines for minor violations
exceptions: Official government statements
State media reporting
Military personnel communications through official channels

quiz.q: What term became illegal to use in Russia to describe the Ukraine conflict under 2022 censorship laws?
quiz.explanation: Russia's censorship laws made it illegal to call the Ukraine conflict a war, requiring use of the term special military operation instead, with up to 15 years imprisonment for violations.

laws.title: Russia Annexation of Ukrainian Territories and Legal Integration
laws.subtitle: Russia illegally annexes four Ukrainian regions and integrates them into Russian law
laws.fullDescription: In September 2022, Russia conducted sham referenda in four Ukrainian regions (Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson) and declared their annexation into Russia. Russian law was subsequently extended to these territories, including Russian criminal law, conscription obligations, and administrative systems. The annexation was declared illegal under international law by the UN General Assembly. Ukraine and most of the world do not recognize the annexations.
laws.penalty: Resistance to Russian administration in annexed territories treated as treason or sabotage; conscription evasion carries criminal penalties
exceptions: Ukrainian citizens who flee occupied territories retain Ukrainian legal status
International humanitarian law protects civilian rights in occupied territories
Diplomatic personnel retain immunities

quiz.q: How many Ukrainian regions did Russia attempt to annex in September 2022?
quiz.explanation: Russia conducted sham referenda in four Ukrainian regions — Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson — and declared their annexation in September 2022, a move declared illegal by the UN General Assembly.

laws.title: Russia Constitutional Amendments — Putin's Extended Rule
laws.subtitle: Russia's 2020 constitutional amendments allow Putin to rule until 2036
laws.fullDescription: Russia's 2020 constitutional amendments, approved in a referendum, reset Vladimir Putin's presidential term count to zero, allowing him to seek re-election in 2024 and potentially rule until 2036. The amendments also added provisions subordinating Russian courts to constitutional provisions over international treaties, prohibiting calls for territorial separation, and adding traditional family values language. Putin was re-elected in March 2024 with 87% of the vote in an election without genuine opposition.
laws.penalty: Calling for separation of Russian territory: criminal offense; challenging the constitutional provisions in court: not possible as the Constitutional Court was restructured
exceptions: Legitimate discussion of constitutional provisions is technically permitted
International law obligations are formally maintained while subordinated to the constitution
Regional governance rights are maintained within federal structure

quiz.q: Until what year could Russia's 2020 constitutional amendments allow Putin to remain in power?
quiz.explanation: Russia's 2020 constitutional amendments reset Putin's presidential term count, allowing him to be re-elected in 2024 and potentially rule until 2036 — meaning he could serve as Russian president for over 35 years in total.

laws.title: Sovereign Internet (Runet) Law
laws.subtitle: Russia's law enabling isolation of domestic internet
laws.fullDescription: Russia's Sovereign Internet Law (Runet law) requires Russian internet service providers to install deep packet inspection equipment provided and controlled by Roskomnadzor (the federal communications regulator). This enables Russian authorities to filter foreign internet traffic, redirect domestic traffic within Russia without using foreign infrastructure, and potentially isolate the entire Russian internet from the global internet. The law mandates routing through state-approved exchange points. Following the Ukraine invasion, Russia dramatically accelerated implementation, blocking or slowing access to thousands of foreign sites.
laws.penalty: Providers failing to install required filtering equipment face fines and ultimately loss of operating licenses; operating VPN services without proper registration and cooperation with blocking orders carries fines
exceptions: Diplomatic missions have protected communications channels
State security services operate outside the filtering system
Critical infrastructure has modified requirements

quiz.q: What does Russia's Sovereign Internet Law enable authorities to do with Russian internet traffic in extreme cases?
options: Isolate the entire Russian internet from the global internet
Require real-name registration for all accounts
quiz.explanation: Russia's Sovereign Internet Law creates the technical infrastructure to completely isolate Russian internet traffic from the global internet, operating it as a domestic-only network if authorities choose.

laws.title: Wartime Mobilization Legal Framework
laws.subtitle: Russia's laws governing military conscription and wartime obligations
laws.fullDescription: Russia enacted extensive legal changes following the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, including laws authorizing partial mobilization of reservists, creating severe criminal penalties for spreading false information about the military, refusing to participate in hostilities, or voluntarily surrendering. Desertion and insubordination penalties were significantly increased. Anti-war protests were effectively criminalized. A new offense of discrediting the armed forces carried up to 15 years for repeat violations. Draft-eligible men faced exit restrictions during mobilization periods.
laws.penalty: Spreading false information about the military carries up to 15 years imprisonment; desertion during combat operations carries 5 to 15 years; voluntary surrender carries 3 to 10 years; discrediting the armed forces carries up to 5 years
exceptions: Sole breadwinners and those with multiple dependents may qualify for deferral
Medical exemptions apply for documented serious health conditions
IT professionals in critical sectors received temporary deferments

quiz.q: What offense did Russia create specifically to silence criticism of its military operations in Ukraine?
quiz.explanation: Russia created a new offense of discrediting the armed forces, carrying up to 15 years imprisonment for repeat violations, specifically designed to criminalize public criticism of Russian military operations in Ukraine.

laws.title: Foreign Agent and Undesirable Organizations Laws
laws.subtitle: Russia's expanding restrictions on civil society and foreign-connected entities
laws.fullDescription: Russia has dramatically expanded its Foreign Agent law and Undesirable Organizations legislation, effectively eliminating independent civil society. Individuals and organizations that receive foreign funding or are deemed to be acting in foreign interests must register as foreign agents, label all their communications, and submit to extensive audits. Hundreds of organizations and individuals have been designated. The Undesirable Organizations law bans foreign and international NGOs and makes participation in their activities a criminal offense even if conducted abroad. Memorial (Russia's oldest human rights organization) was forcibly liquidated.
laws.penalty: Operating as a foreign agent without registration carries fines and criminal charges of up to 2 years; participating in activities of undesirable organizations carries up to 6 years; failure to label foreign agent materials carries fines
exceptions: State-approved entities that receive foreign funding through approved channels are exempt
Religious organizations of registered faiths have partial exemptions
Russian state enterprises with foreign partners follow commercial law rather than foreign agent rules

quiz.q: What happened to Memorial, Russia's oldest human rights organization, under the expanding foreign agent laws?
options: It was fined heavily and continued operating
Its foreign funding was cut off
It was forcibly liquidated by court order
quiz.explanation: Memorial, Russia's oldest and most respected human rights organization which had documented Soviet-era repression and current human rights abuses, was forcibly liquidated by Russian court order in 2021-2022, a symbol of the effective elimination of independent civil society under expanding foreign agent legislation.

laws.title: Russia Presidential Election 2024 and Wartime Constitutional Order
laws.subtitle: Putin's fifth term in an election with no genuine competition
laws.fullDescription: Russia held a presidential election in March 2024, resulting in Vladimir Putin winning a fifth term with 87% of the vote — a result widely characterized by international observers as neither free nor fair. All credible opposition was excluded, imprisoned, or dead (Alexei Navalny died in an Arctic prison in February 2024). The election occurred amid Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine, with wartime economic and security laws in effect, including expanded treason and 'discrediting the army' offenses. Conscription systems were further reformed.
laws.penalty: 'Discrediting the army' (spreading information contradicting official military accounts): fines of RUB 30,000–100,000 for first offense; up to 5 years imprisonment for repeat violations. Calling the war a 'war' rather than 'special military operation' constitutes an offense.
exceptions: Foreign journalists with accreditation face deportation rather than criminal prosecution for first violations
Academic publications on military affairs with prior FSB review may discuss operations with modified terminology

quiz.q: What happened to opposition leader Alexei Navalny shortly before Russia's 2024 presidential election?
options: He died in an Arctic prison in February 2024
He was allowed to run but received less than 1% of the vote
quiz.explanation: Alexei Navalny, Russia's most prominent opposition leader, died in an Arctic penal colony in February 2024, shortly before the March 2024 presidential election. His death, widely attributed to the prison conditions and treatment, drew international condemnation.

laws.title: Russia Oil Price Cap Evasion and Shadow Fleet
laws.subtitle: Sanctions circumvention through non-Western tanker fleet
laws.fullDescription: Following Western oil price caps ($60/barrel for Russian crude) imposed in December 2022, Russia developed an extensive 'shadow fleet' of oil tankers — aging vessels operating outside Western insurance and financial systems — to continue exporting oil at prices above the cap to non-Western buyers. By 2024, the shadow fleet had grown to an estimated 600+ vessels. G7 countries imposed secondary sanctions on financial institutions in third countries that facilitated above-cap Russian oil purchases.
laws.penalty: Western entities that violate Russia oil price cap sanctions face civil penalties of up to $1 million per transaction and criminal prosecution. Third-country banks that facilitate above-cap transactions risk being cut off from US correspondent banking.
exceptions: Oil used for humanitarian purposes (food production, heating) in certain jurisdictions received case-by-case exemptions
Pipeline oil (not transported by sea) subject to separate bilateral agreements with EU pipeline recipients

quiz.q: Approximately how many vessels were estimated to be in Russia's shadow tanker fleet by 2024?
quiz.explanation: Russia's shadow fleet of oil tankers — vessels operating outside Western insurance and financial systems to bypass oil price caps — had grown to an estimated 600+ vessels by 2024, enabling Russia to continue exporting oil above the G7's $60 per barrel price cap to non-Western buyers.

laws.title: Russia Foreign Agents and Undesirable Organizations Expansion
laws.subtitle: Cracking down on civil society and international NGOs
laws.fullDescription: Russia continued expanding its 'foreign agent' laws in 2023–2024, lowering thresholds for designation and expanding categories of restricted activities. Any organization or individual receiving foreign funding or deemed to be 'under foreign influence' could be designated a foreign agent, requiring burdensome reporting, labeling on all communications, and restricting funding. 'Undesirable organizations' (including many Western foundations and NGOs) were banned entirely, with criminal penalties for those who maintain contacts.
laws.penalty: Foreign agent designation violations (failing to label materials, improper reporting): fines up to RUB 500,000 and imprisonment up to 5 years. Participating in an 'undesirable organization': imprisonment up to 6 years.
exceptions: State-affiliated organizations receiving foreign cultural grants under approved bilateral programs may apply for exemption
Academic institutions with state certification for international research partnerships may receive modified treatment

quiz.q: What designation allows Russia to ban international organizations entirely, with criminal penalties for maintaining contacts?
quiz.explanation: Russia's 'undesirable organization' designation is the more severe category, banning organizations entirely and imposing criminal penalties of up to 6 years imprisonment for anyone who maintains contacts with them — unlike the 'foreign agent' designation which restricts but doesn't ban. Many Western foundations and NGOs have been designated undesirable.

laws.title: Partial Mobilisation and War Censorship Laws
laws.subtitle: Russia criminalizes 'discrediting' the military and calling the war a war
laws.fullDescription: Russia enacted laws criminalizing 'discrediting' the Russian Armed Forces and spreading 'false information' about military operations, making it illegal to call the Ukraine invasion a war (the state termed it a 'Special Military Operation'). A partial mobilisation order in September 2022 called up 300,000 reservists. Anti-mobilisation protests led to mass arrests. Independent media were forced to close or leave Russia.
laws.penalty: Discrediting the military: up to 7 years; spreading 'false information' about military: up to 15 years; repeated anti-war protests: criminal charges
exceptions: Diplomatic communications maintain protections
State-approved journalists embed with military under special accreditation

quiz.q: What term did Russia's government legally mandate instead of 'war' when referring to the Ukraine invasion?
quiz.explanation: Russian law effectively banned calling the invasion a 'war' — the official state term was 'Special Military Operation' (специальная военная операция), and using 'war' could constitute spreading false information.

laws.title: Arctic Energy Expansion and Sanctions Evasion Laws
laws.subtitle: Russia expands Arctic oil production while circumventing Western sanctions
laws.fullDescription: Russia enacted legislation expanding Arctic energy development rights and creating legal frameworks for sanctions circumvention through third-country routing of exports. The laws facilitated continued oil and gas exports through shadow fleets, created special economic zones in the Russian Far East with reduced reporting requirements, and restricted foreign companies' ability to exit Russian investments.
laws.penalty: Companies that assist in enforcing Western sanctions against Russian entities: criminal prosecution under Russian counter-sanctions law
exceptions: Humanitarian goods exempted from counter-sanctions provisions
Medical and food imports from sanctioning countries permitted through licensed channels

quiz.q: What method did Russia primarily use to continue exporting oil despite Western sanctions?
quiz.explanation: Russia primarily used shadow fleets — tankers operating without conventional Western insurance or registration — and routing exports through third countries to continue crude oil and refined product sales despite Western sanctions.

laws.title: Russian Energy Pivot to Asia and Yuan Trade
laws.subtitle: Russia restructures trade toward China after Western sanctions
laws.fullDescription: Russia enacted laws facilitating trade and energy contracts denominated in Chinese yuan, Indian rupees, and other non-Western currencies. Pipeline infrastructure for gas exports to China was expanded. New legislation required major Russian exporters to convert a percentage of foreign earnings to rubles. Russia-China trade reached record levels, with China becoming Russia's largest trading partner.
laws.penalty: Russian companies failing to repatriate required percentage of export earnings: Central Bank fines; sanctions violations by Russian entities: criminal prosecution under counter-sanctions law
exceptions: Small exporters below threshold exempt from mandatory repatriation requirements
Defence-sector exports have separate classified accounting frameworks

quiz.q: What currency became increasingly used in Russia-China trade after Western sanctions?
quiz.explanation: The Chinese yuan (renminbi) became increasingly dominant in Russia-China trade after Western sanctions cut Russia off from the dollar-dominated financial system, with bilateral trade shifting almost entirely to yuan and ruble settlements.

laws.title: Russia War Economy Legislation and Mobilization Laws
laws.subtitle: Legal framework for prolonged military operations
laws.fullDescription: Russia's State Duma enacted comprehensive war economy legislation in 2025-2026 including the Defence Industry Mobilization Act requiring civilian manufacturers to accept military production orders, the Counter-Sanction Retaliation Law authorizing asset seizure of Western company assets remaining in Russia, and amendments to the Administrative Code criminalizing 'discrediting' military operations with fines up to 5 million rubles for first offense. The Digital Sovereignty Act mandated disconnection capability from global internet infrastructure. Corporate governance of nationalized Western assets transferred to Rostec and Rosneft management.
laws.penalty: Refusing military production order: up to 10 years imprisonment for executives; 'discrediting' military: 5 million rubles first offense, 7 years imprisonment for repeat; sharing information contradicting official military statistics: 15 years imprisonment
exceptions: Small enterprises with under 50 employees exempt from military production mandates
Medical and pharmaceutical manufacturers have modified compliance framework
Religious organizations exempt from certain political speech restrictions

quiz.q: What maximum fine does Russia's Administrative Code impose for 'discrediting' military operations as a first offense?
quiz.explanation: Russia's Administrative Code amendments set fines up to 5 million rubles for a first offense of 'discrediting' military operations, with repeat offenses potentially resulting in imprisonment up to 7 years.

laws.title: Russia Digital Sovereignty and Internet Isolation Framework
laws.subtitle: Runet expansion and foreign platform restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Russia enacted the Digital Sovereignty Consolidation Act 2025, completing the technical and legal infrastructure for the 'Runet' — Russia's partially isolated domestic internet. The law requires all internet service providers to install deep packet inspection equipment connected to Roskomnadzor's centralized control system, mandates that all messaging applications operating in Russia store data on Russian servers and provide encryption keys to FSB upon request, bans VPN services that cannot demonstrate cooperation with government filtering requirements, establishes criminal penalties for operating blocked platforms, and requires Russian government agencies to migrate to domestic software alternatives for all sensitive functions. International technology companies faced a choice between compliance and market exit.
laws.penalty: Operating blocked platform: 15 years imprisonment for Russian representatives; VPN non-compliance: 10 years; refusing FSB encryption key request: 20 years; foreign software use in sensitive government functions: dismissal plus criminal liability
exceptions: Embassies and diplomatic missions retain access to foreign communication tools
Academic institutions have limited exemption for international research collaboration
Medical and humanitarian organizations have modified framework for foreign platform use

quiz.q: What is the name for Russia's partially isolated domestic internet that the 2025 Digital Sovereignty Act further develops?
quiz.explanation: 'Runet' is the informal name for Russia's domestic internet infrastructure, being developed as a partially isolated system that can be disconnected from the global internet — the infrastructure that the Digital Sovereignty Consolidation Act further develops.

laws.title: Russia Arctic Oil Pivot and China-India Energy Partnership Law
laws.subtitle: Redirecting petroleum exports amid Western sanctions
laws.fullDescription: Russia enacted the Arctic Energy Sovereignty and Eastern Energy Partnership Act 2025, formalizing the redirection of Russian energy exports from Europe to China and India following Western sanctions. The law establishes the Russian Arctic Energy Authority governing Yamal LNG, Arctic LNG 2, and future development projects using indigenous Russian technology (replacing Western equipment), creates preferential payment frameworks in yuan and rupees for Chinese and Indian energy purchasers, provides regulatory framework for the Northern Sea Route as Russian-administered international commercial shipping lane, authorizes development of Arctic seabed reserves using Russian-developed ice-resistant drilling technology, and establishes RUSGAS International as state trading company for global LNG marketing.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized Northern Sea Route navigation without Russian icebreaker escort: vessel detention; Arctic energy contract breach: international arbitration under Russian commercial arbitration framework; sanctions evasion detection (ironic): regulatory violation
exceptions: Scientific research vessels from non-sanctioning nations may navigate NSR under simplified permit
Emergency maritime search and rescue has priority over commercial navigation rules
Environmental monitoring infrastructure exempt from commercial energy development permits

quiz.q: Which two major Asian countries became Russia's primary energy customers after Western sanctions cut off European markets?
quiz.explanation: China and India became Russia's primary energy customers after Western sanctions following the Ukraine invasion significantly reduced Russian energy sales to Europe — a fundamental redirection of global energy flows that Russia's Arctic Energy Partnership Act formalizes.

laws.title: Wartime Economy and Military Mobilization Continuity Act
laws.subtitle: Ongoing Ukraine war economic and military legal framework
laws.fullDescription: Russia has enacted sweeping legislation codifying its wartime economic management, including mandatory defense industry production quotas, restrictions on capital outflows, criminalization of anti-war speech, and enhanced conscription powers. The law formalizes the hybrid war economy that has developed since 2022, legally compelling civilian enterprises to prioritize defense contracts and expanding grounds for mobilization of reservists.
laws.penalty: Anti-war speech or spreading 'false information' about military operations carries up to 15 years imprisonment. Refusal of mobilization call-up carries up to 10 years. Corporate non-compliance with defense production orders carries heavy fines and potential nationalization.
exceptions: Sole breadwinners of families with three or more children under 18 may defer mobilization
Workers in certain critical civilian infrastructure sectors are exempt from production reassignment orders

quiz.q: What does Russia's Wartime Economy Act criminalize with up to 15 years imprisonment?
options: Spreading false information about military operations
quiz.explanation: The law criminalizes spreading 'false information' about military operations — widely applied to any anti-war speech — with up to 15 years in prison.

laws.title: Presidential Continuity and Constitutional Entrenchment Act
laws.subtitle: Putin term reset and permanent rule consolidation
laws.fullDescription: Russia enacted legislation further entrenching President Putin's rule following his 2024 re-election to a sixth term. The law interprets the 2020 constitutional amendments that reset Putin's term count to allow him to stand for election again in 2030 and 2036 if he chooses, effectively making him president-for-life. It also expands the grounds for which Russian citizenship may be stripped from critics abroad and creates new crimes related to 'discrediting state symbols.'
laws.penalty: Discrediting state symbols including the flag, anthem, and the concept of the special military operation carries up to eight years. Russian citizens abroad who collaborate with foreign governments face citizenship revocation. Critics who 'undermine Russia's constitutional order' face up to 20 years.
exceptions: Religious ceremonies may display flags of religious organizations without triggering state symbol restrictions
Russian diaspora cultural events retain permission to display historical Russian flags including pre-Soviet era flags

quiz.q: How many years could Vladimir Putin theoretically remain as president under Russia's constitutional interpretation?
options: As long as he lives and wins elections
quiz.explanation: Under Russia's constitutional interpretation after the 2020 amendments reset Putin's term count, he could theoretically stand for election in 2030 and 2036, potentially remaining president until 2036 or beyond — effectively for as long as he wishes.

laws.title: Ceasefire Negotiation Framework and Territorial Annexation Act
laws.subtitle: Legalizing occupied Ukrainian territories
laws.fullDescription: Russia enacted legislation cementing its position on annexed Ukrainian territories of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson oblasts. The law establishes administrative frameworks for the occupied regions, integrates them into Russian legal, tax, and social systems, and creates the Russian government's legal position for any ceasefire negotiations — that Russia will not accept return of these territories. It also creates provisions for Russian settlers in occupied areas.
laws.penalty: Residents of occupied territories who resist integration into Russian administrative systems face prosecution under Russian law. Those who maintain Ukrainian citizenship while in occupied territories face deportation or prosecution.
exceptions: Civilians who fled to Ukrainian-controlled territory before the annexations are not subject to immediate Russian citizenship requirements
International humanitarian organizations operating in occupied areas retain limited legal status under international humanitarian law frameworks

quiz.q: How many Ukrainian regions did Russia declare annexed in September 2022?
quiz.explanation: In September 2022, Russia declared the annexation of four Ukrainian regions — Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson — in violation of international law. This was in addition to Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea, which is not internationally recognized.

laws.title: Arctic Nuclear Power and Floating Reactor Expansion Act
laws.subtitle: Powering remote Arctic development with floating nuclear plants
laws.fullDescription: Russia enacted legislation expanding its program of floating nuclear power plants and small modular reactors for Arctic energy needs. The law authorizes construction of four new floating nuclear power units, creates regulations for Arctic SMR deployment at remote mining and LNG facilities, establishes liability frameworks for nuclear operations in the environmentally sensitive Arctic, and creates export frameworks for selling Russian Arctic nuclear technology internationally.
laws.penalty: Nuclear safety violations in Arctic floating plants carry up to 30 years imprisonment given the environmental sensitivity. Unauthorized export of nuclear technology to sanctioned countries carries life imprisonment.
exceptions: Domestic research reactors retain their existing operational frameworks
Nuclear submarines and military naval reactors operate under separate military law

quiz.q: What is the name of Russia's first floating nuclear power plant that began operations in the Arctic?
quiz.explanation: Akademik Lomonosov is Russia's first floating nuclear power plant, named after the famous Russian scientist. It was towed to Pevek in Chukotka in the Russian Far Arctic in 2019 and began supplying electricity and heat to the remote community.

laws.title: Russia Wartime Economy and Strategic Industry Mobilization Act
laws.subtitle: Defense Industrial Complex Priority Law
laws.fullDescription: Formally restructures Russia's economy around wartime priorities, requiring civilian industries to accept defense production orders, establishing priority resource allocation for the military-industrial complex, creating labor mobilization mechanisms for defense factories, and establishing legal frameworks for managing the economy under Western sanctions. The law reflects Russia's transition to a permanent wartime economic footing.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for enterprises refusing defense production orders; up to 10 years for sabotage of defense production
exceptions: Small businesses under 50 employees may be exempt from forced defense orders
Medical and food production facilities have protected civilian priority status

quiz.q: What does Russia's Wartime Economy Act require civilian industries to accept?
quiz.explanation: Russia's Wartime Economy Act requires civilian industries to accept defense production orders as Russia shifted to a wartime economic footing.

laws.title: Russia Cryptocurrency Sanctions Evasion and Digital Ruble Act
laws.subtitle: State Digital Currency and Crypto Regulation Law
laws.fullDescription: Regulates cryptocurrency to prevent Western sanctions evasion while establishing the digital ruble as Russia's official central bank digital currency. The law criminalizes use of certain foreign cryptocurrencies for international transactions, creates the digital ruble framework for retail and wholesale payments, establishes licensing for domestic crypto exchanges serving Russian clients, and mandates CBDC integration with government payments.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for using cryptocurrency to evade sanctions; up to 7 years imprisonment
exceptions: Cryptocurrency mining for export remains permitted in designated energy-surplus regions
Licensed exchanges operating within Russia under state oversight

quiz.q: What official digital currency is Russia establishing under its Cryptocurrency Act?
quiz.explanation: Russia's act establishes the digital ruble as Russia's official central bank digital currency alongside regulating other cryptocurrencies.

laws.title: Russia Ceasefire Negotiations and Post-War Reconstruction Framework Act
laws.subtitle: Ukraine Peace Process and Occupied Territory Law
laws.fullDescription: Establishes Russia's legal framework for potential ceasefire negotiations and the governance of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories. The law creates the legal basis for Russian administration of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson oblasts, establishes reconstruction frameworks for war-damaged areas under Russian control, creates legal systems for occupied populations, and establishes Russia's negotiating positions.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for resistance to Russian administration in occupied areas; up to life imprisonment
exceptions: Humanitarian workers have limited protected status
International organizations have supervised access to assess conditions

quiz.q: How many Ukrainian oblasts has Russia claimed to have annexed since 2022?
quiz.explanation: Russia has claimed to annex four Ukrainian oblasts: Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson, though it does not fully control all of these territories.

laws.title: Russia Political Prisoners and Navalny Legacy Commemoration Law
laws.subtitle: Opposition Suppression and Civil Society Control Act
laws.fullDescription: Documents Russia's treatment of political prisoners and the legal framework suppressing civil society. Following Alexei Navalny's death in a Russian prison in February 2024, the law creates enhanced penalties for participating in organizations deemed extremist, strengthens foreign agent legislation, creates new censorship mechanisms, and establishes asset seizure for anti-government activity. International condemnation continues.
laws.penalty: Up to 25 years imprisonment for extremism; asset confiscation; up to 7 years for spreading military disinformation
exceptions: State-approved civil society organizations operate within restrictions
Russian Orthodox Church maintains independence within controlled sphere

quiz.q: What prominent Russian opposition figure died in a Russian prison in February 2024?
quiz.explanation: Alexei Navalny, Russia's most prominent opposition leader, died in a Russian Arctic prison in February 2024 in circumstances widely blamed on the Kremlin.

laws.title: War Economy Transformation and NATO Response
laws.subtitle: Russia Puts Economy on Full Military Footing
laws.fullDescription: Russia transformed to a war economy with defense spending exceeding 6% of GDP by 2024-25, the highest since the Soviet era. Labor shortages from military mobilization and emigration were offset by wage increases and automation. Western sanctions redirected trade to China, India, and other partners, but long-term economic damage accelerated.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for draft evasion; economic conscription through labor market
exceptions: Military deferment categories
Alternative service provisions limited

quiz.q: What percentage of GDP did Russia's defense spending reach by 2024-25?
quiz.explanation: Russia's defense spending exceeded 6% of GDP by 2024-25, the highest since the Soviet era, as the country fully transitioned to a war economy.

laws.title: LGBT Propaganda Laws and International Sports Ban
laws.subtitle: Russia Expands Criminalization of LGBTQ Visibility
